title: Functions, recursion and structures
subtitle: Break a big problem into named pieces, and group related data into one unit.

fn.title: Defining and calling functions
fn.body: A function has a return type, name, parameters and body: int square(int x) { return x * x; }. Declare a prototype before use so the compiler knows the signature. void functions return nothing. Benefits: reuse, testing one piece at a time, readability.

scope.title: Scope and lifetime
scope.body: Local variables live inside a function (or block) and vanish when it returns; each call has its own copy. Global variables are visible everywhere but make code harder to reason about. static locals keep their value between calls.

stack.title: The call stack
stack.body: Each call pushes a stack frame holding parameters, locals and the return address; return pops it. Recursion simply stacks many frames.

rec.title: Recursion vs iteration
rec.body: Anything recursive can be written with a loop. Recursion is natural for trees and divide-and-conquer; iteration is cheaper (no frames). The naive recursive Fibonacci recomputes subproblems: fib(6) makes 25 calls.

struct.title: Structures
struct.body: A struct bundles fields of different types: struct Student { int roll; int marks; };. Access with the dot operator (s.marks), or arrow through a pointer (p->marks). Assigning one struct to another copies every field.
struct.steps: struct { char c; int i; } on a typical machine: c takes 1 byte, then 3 bytes of padding so i is 4-aligned. Total size 1 + 3 + 4.

union.title: Arrays of structs, unions, enums
union.body: An array of structs models a table (students). A union shares one memory slot between its members (size = largest member). enum gives names to integer constants (enum {RED, GREEN, BLUE}; = 0, 1, 2). typedef creates a shorter type name.
